deep.reconstruction:
This page has no text. It is a single pencil sketch in the upper-left corner; everything else is show-through from the other side of the sheet. The sketch fits the surrounding pages (107, 109), which study how one pseudo-line, a 'curve', is deformed across the crossing points of an arrangement of pseudo-lines.

What is drawn:
- Two pairs of almost straight lines, each pair forming an X. Call the crossing points P1 (left X, roughly at image coordinates (340,230)) and P2 (right X, roughly at (590,350)).
- A nearly horizontal line passing just below P1 and just above P2.
- A sinuous curve starting top-left, passing above P1, descending, crossing the horizontal line once between the two X's, and passing below P2.

Interpretation in modern terms:
- The horizontal line and the sinuous curve are two positions of a sweeping pseudo-line, or two pseudo-lines, relative to the 4-line arrangement.
- The horizontal line has P1 above it and P2 below it. The curve does the reverse: P1 below, P2 above.
- Passing from one to the other therefore means pushing the curve across both vertices P1 and P2. Each such passage is an elementary move: a triangle flip or 'mutation', i.e. a Reidemeister-III-type move.
- The single crossing between the two curves reflects this change of side.

What problem it serves: the combinatorics of how a pseudo-line, or a sweep line, can be homotoped through an arrangement. This is the setting of Ringel's homotopy theorem and of the topological sweep / wiring diagram descriptions of arrangements. It continues the page-107 figures, where a green curve 'bumps up over the first crossing' between abscissae x0 and x1.

The page contains no claims, notation or computations; it is an exploratory figure.

ideas.what: Deforming a pseudo-line across crossing points of an arrangement, one vertex at a time (elementary flips), to pass between two positions that place the vertices on opposite sides
ideas.modern_name: Triangle flips / mutations of pseudo-line arrangements; Ringel's homotopy theorem; topological sweep of arrangements
ideas.usually_credited_to: G. Ringel (1956); J.E. Goodman (wiring diagrams, 1980); Edelsbrunner–Guibas (topological sweep, 1986)
ideas.where_published: Not in published texts; the pseudo-line material survives only in the Montpellier archive (cote 154)

deep.surprise_reason: A wordless exploratory sketch of a curve passing above one crossing and below another in a small pseudo-line configuration. It is standard combinatorial geometry with no new claim visible.
transcription_corrections: The sinuous curve passes above the left crossing and below the right crossing, crossing the near-horizontal line once between the two X's; the horizontal line itself passes below the left crossing and above the right one.
The short dark dashes and faint letter-like marks (V/A shapes, hooked strokes) across the rest of the sheet are show-through from the reverse side, not content of this page.
